dehydrated_text:
Well, what are you going to give me? I'm going to give you gold, right? So, I take the receipt and give it to you. And why do we do this? Because it's easier than giving gold directly to others. This system would facilitate trade throughout the world.

So, as a bank, I have all this gold and want to make money with it. Other merchants come to me and say, "I need gold. Can you lend me some?" But if I give out the gold, they might have security issues. So why don't I give them a receipt or contract instead? Because all I need is that receipt to do trade elsewhere.

By doing this, I've doubled the amount of gold in my bank—5 million in gold plus 5 million in receipts. Now theoretically, I have 10 million in total. This is how money and finance work.

Now there's a problem with this system. Why would other people trust me to give them gold? For most of human history, people didn't need money. If you were just a normal person, you traded directly—like trading a cow for something else. So, we didn't actually need money until certain circumstances like marriage or settling disputes.

In these cases, money represented unpaid debt that could never be repaid. For example, if I killed someone, their family might accept money as compensation. Money was symbolic and used to settle disputes.

With the rise of trade, merchants needed money but trusted each other. So money served as a mechanism for easier trade among known parties.

However, there's a problem here: can receipts be forged? This is a great question because if people start forging contracts, it could cause issues.

The bigger issue lies in bank runs. If everyone wants to redeem their gold at the same time, I'll go bankrupt because I only have 5 million in gold and 10 million in contracts. Only if 15 million want their gold back will I face a severe problem called a bank run. This is a huge risk for merchants.

Another issue is who I lend my money to. Usually, I would lend it to other merchants or individuals who need capital for trade.
